messages.subject: Re: AIC from fitqtl
messages.body_plain:
Whether it would be appropriate is unclear, but you can always
calculate the AIC from the result of fitqtl.

Basically, if the LOD score corresponding to a model fittedd by fitqtl
is L, then AIC will be
   -2*log(10)*L + 2*df,
where df is the degrees of freedom of the model.

In the context of QTL problems, Karl's investigations have shown that
a BIC-type penalty might be better.

I'll let Karl elaborate.

Saunak

messages.subject: Re: AIC from fitqtl
messages.body_plain:
The fitqtl function provides a log likelihood for a model (or, with
the drop-one-term analysis,
for a set of models).  One can obtain AIC values from that by
subtracting the appropriate
penalty.

However, there's no reason to prefer the particular penalty in AIC;
it is derived by an asymptotic
argument and may not be behaved appropriately in regular-sized
samples.  We are working on extending
our previous work on additive QTL models to the case that
interactions are to be considered, but
we're not quite there yet, and so I don't yet have advice concerning
criteria for comparing models.

karl

messages.subject_clean: Display all LOD results from scanone or scantwo in table
messages.body_plain:
A quick question: summary.scanone and summary.scantwo produce
summaries of the maximum points of significance for analysis for a
given chromosome or combination and one can tailor the LOD thresholds
to be illustrated, but is there syntax that allows the collection of
ALL lod scores at all points along the chromosome or within a
combination?  I'm looking in the manual but can't seem to find it.
Presumably there must exist some summary file/table in order to create
the figures for the "plot" statement, but how does one access it?

Sincerely

G Perry

messages.subject: Re: Double haploid population
messages.body_plain:
You can treat the data as a backcross.  If you are reading the data in
the CSV
format you can specify that by something like this:

cr <-
read.cross(format="csv",dir=".",file="myfile.csv",genotypes=c("AA","BB"))

This will tell R/qtl that the second genotype "BB" is to be treated as
a het, and
since the other homozygote is not present, will think it is a
backcross.

Saunak

messages.subject: Re: Display all LOD results from scanone or scantwo in table
messages.subject_clean: Display all LOD results from scanone or scantwo in table
messages.body_plain:
For the output of scanone, you can use write.table to send the results
to a file.  For example:

   > data(hyper)
   > hyper <- calc.genoprob(hyper, step=2)
   > out <- scanone(hyper)
   > write.table(out, file="output.csv", sep=",")

The output of scantwo is more complicated.  For example, consider the
following, where we have a 2d scan of just chromosomes 6 and 15:

   > data(hyper)
   > hyper <- calc.genoprob(hyper, step=5)
   > out <- scantwo(hyper, chr=c(6,15))

out$lod is a 26x26 matrix, with values along the diagonal being the
results of scanone, those in the upper-right triangle being the
LOD scores comparing a two-locus additive model to the null and those
in the lower-left triangle being the LOD scores comparing the two-locus
full (including interaction) model to the null.

out$map contains information about the positions at which the LOD scores
were calculated.

How to send this to a file?  You could send each of out$lod and out$map
to a comma-delimited file using write.table, if you want.

karl
